title: Physical fitness changes following group-based interval small-sided games among middle school soccer players
venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
abstract: Objective: This study examined changes in aerobic fitness, resting and exercise heart rates, and sprint performance following an eight-week interval-based small-sided games program among middle school students participating in extracurricular soccer. Methods: Twenty-four male students from SMP Negeri 6 Palu, Indonesia, participated in a one-group pretest–posttest study involving 24 training sessions. The intervention consisted of 4 vs. 4 small-sided games played on a 30 × 25 m pitch in four 4-min bouts, separated by 2 min of passive recovery. Aerobic fitness was assessed using the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 and expressed as estimated maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max). Heart rate was measured at rest and during exercise, while sprint performance was evaluated using a 30-m sprint test. Pretest and posttest measurements were compared using paired-samples t-tests. Results: Significant pre–post improvements were observed in estimated VO₂max, which increased from 49.82 ± 2.91 to 54.73 ± 3.08 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Resting heart rate decreased from 72.13 ± 4.87 to 67.08 ± 4.12 beats·min⁻¹, while exercise heart rate decreased from 181.46 ± 6.35 to 174.21 ± 5.92 beats·min⁻¹. The 30-m sprint time also improved from 4.82 ± 0.31 to 4.56 ± 0.28 s. All observed differences were statistically significant (p < .001). Conclusion: A systematically structured interval-based small-sided games program was associated with improvements in aerobic fitness, heart-rate responses, and sprint performance among middle school soccer players. This approach may provide a practical and engaging conditioning strategy for school-based extracurricular soccer programs. title: IMPLEMENTATION OF PANCASILA VALUES IN THE DAILY LIVES OF PHYSICAL EDUCATION, HEALTH, AND RECREATION (PJKR) STUDENTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: IMPLEMENTATION OF PANCASILA VALUES IN THE DAILY LIVES OF PHYSICAL EDUCATION, HEALTH, AND RECREATION (PJKR) STUDENTS MUHAMMAD FATIR RACHMAN (289) HAMLAN KHAFIFAN NAURIL ARFAN (294) M. ZIDNY AQLI AQILA MALFARUQ (293) ABSTRACT Pancasila serves as a living philosophy for Indonesians rather than mere theoretical material memorized for examinations. For students enrolled in the Physical Education, Health, and Recreation (PJKR) program, these foundational values hold immense practical relevance across classroom lectures, athletic training, competitive matches, and everyday social interactions. This study explores how PJKR students embody Pancasila principles in their daily routines, specifically focusing on sportsmanship, discipline, tolerance, teamwork, accountability, and equity. Employing a descriptive qualitative methodology through library research, this paper examines literature sourced from academic books, scholarly journals, statutory laws, and articles covering Pancasila, character building, and physical education. The collected data were analyzed systematically via identification, categorization, interpretation, and descriptive synthesis. The findings demonstrate that all five principles of Pancasila integrate seamlessly into student life, manifested through religious tolerance, mutual respect for varying physical capacities, team cohesion, consensus-based decision-making, and equal participation in sports. Consistent practice of these ideals fosters strong personal character and equips students to become ethical physical education teachers. Ultimately, Pancasila must be actively lived in daily actions rather than passively understood in theory. Keywords: Pancasila, PJKR students, physical education, sportsmanship, character education. title: Dimensionality reduction of space-related metrics in elite football using factor analysis
abstract: Spatial organisation is fundamental to understanding football tactics and phase-dependent coordination. However, the high intercorrelation between existing spatial metrics suggests significant redundancy. This study aims to identify the latent dimensions of spatial positioning in- and out-of-possession to refine the theoretical framework of space in professional football. An open-source dataset comprising seven male German Bundesliga matches was utilised to analyse team length, width, height, surface area, convex hull, team centroid, team spread, stretch index, Delaunay triangulation and Voronoi diagram. Ball possession status served as the independent variable. Spearman's rank correlation coefficients were calculated, while data suitability was examined using the KMO statistic and Bartlett's test of sphericity. An exploratory factor analysis was performed to identify underlying latent constructs. High intercorrelation among spatial metrics justified factor analysis to reduce redundancy. The analysis reveals three consistent spatial dimensions that explain team organisation, regardless of possession status. These dimensions account for 77.1% and 75.5% of the variance, respectively, with the first dimension representing almost half of the variance in each case. Factor analysis reduces complex spatial data into three functional dimensions: 'team dispersion', 'longitudinal dispersion', and 'longitudinal positioning'. This facilitates a concise yet comprehensive interpretation of tactical structures and performance analysis.

title: Coach development in esports: Where is the tutorial?
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Coaches play a critical role in athlete development, yet coach development in esports remains limited and undervalued. Despite fulfilling functions similar to those of traditional sports coaches, esports coaches operate in a unique and emerging context, where learning is predominantly self-directed and competitive success is often treated as a proxy for expertise. In this perspective piece, we argue that the lack of engagement with coach development reflects not only limited provision but also a range of social, cultural, and structural constraints. Drawing on Côté and Gilbert's model of coaching effectiveness and Hodkinson and colleagues’ concepts of horizons for action and learning, we examine how time pressures, career precarity, and prevailing learning cultures shape coaches’ decisions.

title: Technical–tactical indicators and point-ending patterns in professional women's doubles pickleball
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Despite the rapid growth of pickleball, evidence-based research on its technical and tactical structure remains limited, especially in doubles play. This study examined technical–tactical indicators and point-ending profiles in professional women's doubles pickleball, with particular attention to spatial control, rally structure, and point resolu-tion. A systematic observational design was applied to 1284 points from 15 semifinal and final matches of five tournaments during the 2023 Professional Pickleball Association Tour. Data were coded using LINCE PLUS and analyzed through descriptive statistics, chi-square tests of independence, Cramer's V, and a descriptive point-ending profile analysis based on selected cases. Points were almost evenly distributed between re-ceiving pairs (52.8%) and serving pairs (47.2%). Most point-ending actions occurred from mid-court areas near the non-volley zone (85.4%), with forehand and backhand volleys as the most frequent finishing strokes. The point-ending profile analysis focused on points whose final stroke was executed from zone 2 and described how rally length, point winner, type of point ending, and final stroke were combined in the most frequent point-resolution situations. Overall, professional women's doubles pickleball appears to be characterized by balanced scoring opportunities, sustained rally exchanges, and point resolution closely associated with spatial control near the non-volley zone and volley execution.

title: Effects of contextual factors on the external workload of top-up training sessions in an elite football team
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: This study aimed to analyse how match location and match outcome affect the external load of top-up sessions in professional football. Forty elite male players from a Spanish first-division team were monitored across 31 top-up sessions during the 2023/2024 competitive season, yielding 628 player-session observations for match-location analyses and 369 player-session observations for match-outcome analyses after excluding drawn matches. External load metrics were obtained via GPS, including total distance, high-speed running (HSR), sprint distance, and the number of accelerations and decelerations. Separate linear mixed-effects models tested location (home/away) and outcome (win/loss), with player as a random effect. Away matches produced longer session duration (F (1, 332) = 15.4, p < .001) with no other differences. Following a loss, sessions showed longer duration (F (1, 197) = 31.4, p < .001), total distance (F (1, 173) = 4.5, p = .036), sprint distance (F (1, 179) = 10.6, p = .001), accelerations >3 m/s 2 (F (1, 174) = 19.4, p < .001), and decelerations >3 m/s 2 (F (1, 170) = 12.5, p < .001), with no differences in high-speed running distance. Marginal R 2 values were low, while conditional R 2 values were higher, reflecting substantial between-player variability. Top-up demands were consistently higher after losses, suggesting that these sessions may be sensitive to competitive context rather than reflecting a stable match replication stimulus. More standardised loading targets may support more consistent weekly load management in underplayed players.

title: Pitch-speed-specific torso–pelvis movement patterns and whole-body joint coordination in baseball pitching
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: This study evaluated continuous torso–pelvis motion in baseball pitchers grouped according to ball speed and examined its kinematic interactions with upper- and lower-extremity joints throughout the pitching motion. Kinematic data were collected from 100 pitchers performing 411 pitches that were classified into three speed-based clusters (C1–C3) using the k-means algorithm. Statistical parametric mapping was used to compare continuous joint kinematics among clusters, and Pearson correlation analyses examined the relationships between significant torso–pelvis motion and upper- and lower-extremity joint motions under pooled and cluster-specific conditions. Compared with C2 (84.64 mph), both C1 (78.39 mph) and C3 (89.58 mph) exhibited significantly greater torso–pelvis extension around ball release. During foot plant time, torso–pelvis motion demonstrated strong correlations (|r| > 0.799) with multiple upper- and lower-extremity joints. However, the number of associated joints of the correlations differed when pitchers were analyzed within individual speed clusters. Evaluating continuous movement patterns throughout the pitching cycle, rather than focusing solely on discrete events such as ball release, may provide a more comprehensive understanding of pitching mechanics and inform performance enhancement and coaching interventions.

title: “You sink or swim”: An investigation into the experiences of applied performance analysts working in women's football
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: Performance analysis research within football has focussed on the outputs of systematic observation, quantification and analysis of performance; less attention has been given to the applied practices of performance analysts. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the experiences of applied performance analysts working within women's football, providing further insight beyond previous initial explorations. Ten performance analysts working with senior women's football teams (international n = 3; top-tier domestic n = 2; second-tier domestic n = 5) in the United Kingdom, participated in semi-structured interviews, which were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Two key themes were developed. Firstly, developing as an applied performance analyst in women's football, with four sub-themes of 1) alignment of learning opportunities to real-world practice, 2) preferences for learning opportunities, 3) navigating internal constraints and 4) navigating external constraints. Secondly, working as an applied performance analyst within women's football, with three sub-themes; 1) prioritisation of performance analysis provision, 2) implementing appropriate performance analysis provision and 3) challenges of working within women's football. The results demonstrate the breadth, depth and complexities of challenges and considerations in becoming, being and developing as an applied performance analyst within women's football. As such, the findings have wide-ranging implications for higher education institutions, academics, and development and learning professionals within football organisations and governing bodies, informing the development of aspiring and current analysts. title: Information retention across judo pause-combat cycles: Effects of high-intensity randori in competitive athletes
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: In judo competition, coaches can provide tactical information only during brief pauses, while athletes must retain and later use relevant information after re-entering high-intensity combat. This proof-of-concept randomized crossover trial tested whether high-intensity randori impairs information retention and retrieval across a judo-like pause-combat cycle. Twenty competitive judo athletes completed a fixed set-size modified Sternberg task in two conditions: rest and high-intensity randori. For 12 trials, participants encoded information, retained it during 20-s periods of rest or randori, and responded after a short return interval. Correct-response time and trial accuracy were analysed using trial-level mixed-effects models. Randori elicited high physiological load, with median heart rate reaching 93.4% of estimated HRmax. Compared with rest, randori produced a model-estimated 10.6% increase in correct-response time (95% CI 1.9 to 20.0; p = .019). Accuracy decreased from 90.0% during rest to 79.6% during randori, with the odds of a correct response reduced by 57% (OR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.73; p = .002). Mental perceived exertion was also higher during randori. These findings suggest that high-intensity judo randori can constrain retention and retrieval of recently encoded neutral information across pause-combat cycles. The study provides a controlled experimental model for future research on coaching instruction timing, cue complexity, and information retention in judo. title: Defensive synergies in association football: A systematic scoping review
venue: International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching
abstract: The evolution of performance analysis in association football, supported by positional tracking, has improved understanding of collective behaviour. However, matches, and the defensive phase, are often summarised through statistics or outcomes. These indicators are poorly sensitive to the emergent organisation of out-of-possession play. From an ecological dynamics perspective, defensive coordination consists of functional couplings between defenders that create synergies reorganising according to task constraints. This scoping review mapped evidence on intra-team defensive synergies in association football following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, including studies published between 01/01/2000 and 01/09/2025 (English/Italian/Spanish/Portuguese/French) that operationalised intra-team defensive coordination and synergies (≥2 defenders). Searches in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, and APA PsycInfo yielded 1217 records; after removing 363 duplicates, 854 records underwent screening and 131 full texts were assessed, resulting in 63 included studies. Common data sources were optical tracking and GPS/GNSS, combined with video/event data. Explicit defensive outcomes were reported in 21/63 studies. Contextual constraints were considered in most studies. The literature is growing, but remains heterogeneous and links between collective properties and defensive outcomes are not systematic. Minimum reporting standards, a core set of metrics, and stronger alignment between coordination measures and process-based outcomes consistent with the out-of-possession phase are needed.

title: Psychological correlates of sport-specific anaerobic performance in kickboxing athletes
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Background Kickboxing is a combat sport that requires repeated high-intensity effort, rapid perceptual-motor responses, and effective self-regulation under pressure. However, the psychological correlates of sport-specific performance in kickboxing remain understudied. Methods This cross-sectional study involved 78 Italian kickboxing athletes who completed self-report measures of tolerance, kickboxing-related self-efficacy, sport engagement, and emotion-related efficacy. A subsample of 60 athletes completed the Kickboxing Anaerobic Speed Test (KAST). Descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, Pearson correlations, and an exploratory multiple linear regression were used. Results KAST completion time was negatively correlated with absorption ( r = −.459), emotion-related efficacy ( r = −.458), kickboxing-related self-efficacy ( r = −.442), empathy ( r = −.432), and vigor ( r = −.342); all five associations remained significant after Holm adjustment across eight comparisons. The exploratory regression explained 38.8% of the observed variance (adjusted R 2 = .343). Kickboxing-related self-efficacy, emotion-related efficacy, and absorption had negative adjusted associations; the empathy coefficient was not statistically significant. Conclusion In this convenience sample, efficacy-related beliefs, vigor, and absorption were associated with completion time on a sport-specific repeated-effort task. The findings are exploratory and do not establish causal effects, prospective predictive accuracy, or the efficacy of psychological interventions.

title: Generational change in Slovenian youth sport participation
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Background Organised sport participation during adolescence provides important physical, psychosocial, and developmental benefits, yet long-term secular trends remain insufficiently understood. This study examined decade-long changes in organised sport participation among Slovenian adolescents using nationally representative repeated cross-sectional data from the Analysis of Children's Development in Slovenia (ACDSi). Methods Data included 5,027 adolescents aged 11–18 years assessed in 2013–2014 and 2023–2024. Organised sport participation, participation history, weekly training volume, sport-category distribution, and physical fitness were analysed overall and by sex and ISCED level. Between-wave differences were tested using Pearson's chi-square tests, and training volume and fitness outcomes using general linear models. Results Organised sport participation increased from 50.4% to 63.4% ( P < .001; OR = 1.71, 95% CI 1.52–1.91), with increases observed in both sexes and both ISCED levels. In the complete-case analysis, previous participation followed by discontinuation was more common in 2023–2024 than in 2013–2014 (27.1% vs. 19.7%), although participation-history data were incomplete for a substantial proportion of 2013–2014 non-participants. Among current participants, adjusted weekly training volume increased from 4.26 to 4.99 h/week in ISCED 2 and from 4.71 to 5.30 h/week in ISCED 3. Sport-category distribution changed modestly across the decade, particularly among girls, while team sports remained the dominant category. Physical fitness differed slightly across sport categories, with the clearest differences observed for standing long-jump and 60-m sprint performance. title: Neuromuscular performance, physiological recovery, and maturation-referenced reference values in youth athletes: A cross-sectional study
abstract: This cross-sectional study characterized neuromuscular performance and acute physiological responses across age, sex, and biological maturation in 140 youth athletes (74 boys, 66 girls; 10–16 years), and described maturation-stratified distributions of two field measures. Participants completed 30-m sprint, countermovement jump (CMJ), standing long jump (SLJ), and handgrip testing; post-sprint heart-rate recovery (HRrec-30s) and a testing-battery perceived-exertion index (PEI) served as co-primary physiological/perceptual outcomes; maturity offset (Mirwald method) classified Pre-, Circa-, and Post-PHV subgroups; allometric scaling was used to account for body size; and a Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction was applied across a pre-specified family of 58 pairwise comparisons and correlations (Tables 2–6). Boys outperformed girls across all neuromuscular tests (d = 0.63–0.76), whereas HRrec-30s and the perceived-exertion index did not differ significantly by sex. HRrec-30s was more strongly associated with maturity offset than with chronological age (r = 0.52 vs 0.46; η²p for maturation vs age groups 0.43 vs 0.39). Mean HRrec-30s was 27.8 ± 6.2 bpm in the Pre-PHV group and 45.3 ± 8.8 bpm in the Post-PHV group (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected). The perceived-exertion index was lower in more mature groups (7.5 ± 1.2 vs 6.3 ± 1.1). Sex and maturation differences in jump and strength performance remained after allometric scaling, although they were smaller. Maturation-stratified distributions reported here are preliminary and descriptive and are not decision thresholds; prospective, criterion-validated research is needed before they can be recommended for individual athlete monitoring or training-load decision-making.
